passage: Three weeks after Bidisha came back from her break, the deadlines came back too. I sit next to her, so I noticed things before she said anything: her laptop still open when I left, the untouched lunchbox, the dark circles returning. On a Tuesday she stood up and knocked on the manager's door. She came out ten minutes later, sat down, and told me quietly she had asked to drop the vendor review from her list. She had also added a weekly counselling session to her calendar, on Wednesday evenings. She did not seem ashamed. She said, "That's just information. It's telling me the plan needs changing." I'm not sure how she felt underneath. She looked tired, but lighter. - Vikas

Monday, 2 June. Urmila's first week back after two months' leave goes well. She sleeps by eleven and wakes rested. She tells her friend Hafsa, "I think I'm actually through it."
Tuesday, 24 June. The product launch is moved up. Urmila is awake at 3 again, running slides in her head. After the third bad night she opens the notebook her counsellor had suggested and writes: "Sleep bad 3 nights. Launch pressure. Same as before." She stares at it. "This is information, not failure," she says out loud, though it doesn't feel that way.
Friday, 27 June. She tells her manager she will step back from leading the partner workshop, and he agrees to give it to Dev. She books a weekly counselling session again, Thursdays at six. That night she texts Hafsa: "Caught it early this time."

qa.q: What did Urmila write in the notebook?
qa.a: "Sleep bad 3 nights. Launch pressure. Same as before."

qa.q: How did Urmila feel when she said "This is information, not failure"?
qa.a: She was trying to stay calm, but part of her still felt disappointed and scared that the old pattern was back.

qa.q: Why is stepping back from the workshop a sensible change?
qa.a: It removes one load just as the launch presses, and together with weekly counselling it treats the bad nights as a signal to act early.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel reading "Caught it early this time"?
qa.a: Hafsa is probably relieved and proud, having heard Urmila hope she was through it only weeks before.

grounding: It shows a woman noticing worse sleep three weeks after returning, telling her manager, dropping a commitment and adding weekly counselling, treating the slip as information.

passage:
Swati Aunty wiped her hands on her dupatta and looked at her niece, who had just said she was back to normal after her leave. "Don't take this wrong. Let me tell you about Shalini, who worked under me at the school office years ago. She took a month off, exhausted, and came back looking well. Three weeks later exam season began, and I noticed she was coming in with puffy eyes, drinking tea after tea.
One afternoon she came to me herself. 'I'm not sleeping again,' she said. 'I think it's starting.' She had already made a plan: she wanted to hand the exam timetable to Revathi, and she had booked a weekly session with a counsellor on Saturdays. I agreed on the spot.
What I remember is that she didn't treat it as failing. She said, 'It's just telling me something.' That's how she got through that season."

qa.q: Who did Shalini want to hand the exam timetable to?
qa.a: She wanted to hand it to Revathi.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she said "I think it's starting"?
qa.a: She was worried the exhaustion was coming back, but calm and clear enough to act on it instead of hiding it.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Shalini through exam season, and why?
qa.a: Going to Swati early with a plan, handing over the timetable and adding weekly counselling, because it treated the bad sleep as a signal rather than a failure.

qa.q: How did Swati see Shalini coming forward?
qa.a: Swati respected it and agreed on the spot, and still remembers that Shalini did not treat it as failing.

grounding: It shows a young woman spotting poor sleep weeks after returning, telling her manager, dropping a task and adding weekly counselling, and treating the relapse as information.
